prompt: Write the introduction section of an academic paper titled “Fixing a Model That Learned Worse Cancer Means Lower Risk: Monotonic Constraints in Bladder Cancer Recurrence Prediction”. The paper is in clinical machine learning. About 700 words. Output only the text of the introduction, with no heading.
raw:
Bladder cancer is among the most common malignancies worldwide, and it is also among the most expensive to manage over a patient's lifetime. Much of that cost comes from recurrence. Most newly diagnosed cases are non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and a large proportion of these tumors recur after transurethral resection, often repeatedly and sometimes with progression to muscle-invasive disease. Patients therefore enter long surveillance regimens built around repeated cystoscopy, urine cytology, and imaging. These procedures are invasive, burdensome, and resource-intensive. Accurate estimates of individual recurrence risk could guide how often patients are surveilled, whether they receive adjuvant intravesical therapy, and when to consider radical treatment. Established instruments such as the EORTC risk tables and the CUETO scoring model are widely used for this purpose. However, they were derived from historical trial cohorts using simple additive scoring, and their discrimination in contemporary populations is frequently reported as modest.

Machine learning models trained on electronic health records, pathology reports, and registry data offer an appealing alternative. Gradient-boosted trees, random forests, and neural survival models can capture nonlinear effects and interactions among clinical variables that point-based scores cannot represent. They can also draw on richer covariates than those available in the original trial datasets. A growing body of work reports that such models can match or exceed traditional risk tables on held-out discrimination metrics. Yet improvements in aggregate performance can conceal a more fundamental problem: a model may learn relationships between individual risk factors and outcome that contradict well-established clinical knowledge.

This paper is motivated by a concrete instance of that problem. In developing a recurrence prediction model for bladder cancer, we observed that a conventionally trained gradient-boosted model assigned *lower* predicted recurrence risk to patients with features universally recognized as markers of more aggressive disease, including higher tumor grade and more advanced stage, over portions of the feature space. Such behavior is not merely an aesthetic flaw. A clinician presented with a prediction that a high-grade tumor carries less risk than an otherwise identical low-grade tumor has good reason to distrust the entire model. If the model were acted upon, it could recommend less intensive surveillance for precisely the patients who need it most.

Counterintuitive associations of this kind are not random artifacts. They arise predictably from the structure of observational clinical data. Patients with high-risk features are more likely to receive intravesical BCG, early repeat resection, or radical cystectomy. These interventions reduce, or in the case of cystectomy effectively eliminate, observable bladder recurrence. Confounding by indication can therefore make aggressive disease appear protective in data where treatment is incompletely recorded or imperfectly modeled. Differences in surveillance intensity, competing risks such as death from other causes, informative censoring, and sparse data in clinically important subgroups can further distort learned relationships. Flexible models exploit whatever statistical regularities exist in the training data, and they have no inherent means of distinguishing a causal relationship from an artifact of how care was delivered.

One principled remedy is to encode domain knowledge directly into the model in the form of monotonic constraints. Under such a constraint, predicted risk is required to be non-decreasing, or non-increasing, in a specified feature while all other features are held fixed. Modern gradient boosting libraries support these constraints natively, and related techniques exist for generalized additive models, lattice models, and neural networks. Monotonicity is a weak assumption in one sense: it does not dictate the shape or magnitude of an effect, only its direction. It is also a powerful assumption, because it rules out exactly the class of clinically implausible behavior that undermines trust. Monotonic constraints have been studied in credit scoring and other regulated domains. Their use in oncology risk prediction, and their interaction with the confounding structures typical of clinical data, has received comparatively little systematic attention.

In this work, we examine the use of monotonic constraints to correct clinically implausible behavior in a bladder cancer recurrence model. We first characterize the non-monotonic relationships learned by an unconstrained model and investigate their likely sources, with particular attention to treatment-related confounding. We then specify monotonicity constraints for a set of risk factors whose directional effects are supported by clinical consensus, and we compare constrained and unconstrained models on discrimination, calibration, and stability across patient subgroups. Finally, we discuss what monotonic constraints can and cannot accomplish. They enforce plausible model behavior and can improve robustness. They do not, however, resolve the underlying confounding, and they should not be mistaken for a causal adjustment. Our aim is to offer a practical template for incorporating clinical knowledge into flexible risk models, so that improved predictive performance does not come at the cost of clinical credibility.
